source.title: Evaluation of AI Solutions in Health Care Organizations - The OPTICA Tool

sourceNote: Paraphrases of the OPTICA checklist, written for this project. The OPTICA paper is NEJM AI 2024, (c) Massachusetts Medical Society, marked 'For personal use only'. Its item text is NOT reproduced here. These are original summaries of each item's intent, with the CHAI crosswalk attached.

sections.title: Defining the clinical need
sections.purpose: Pin down, in concrete terms, the care problem the proposed AI system is supposed to fix, how work is done today versus how it would be done afterwards, what the system must emit, and the measurable bar it has to clear to be worth adopting.

items.text: State the specific care-delivery problem that this system is meant to address.
Describe how this task is handled today — who decides what, at which points, using which information — and spell out the harms, costs, or inefficiencies the status quo produces.

attrs.residue: A documented as-is process map naming each decision point, the role that owns it and the information it relies on, plus an itemized list of status-quo shortcomings (delay, missed or late detection, avoidable cost, unwarranted variation, staff burden) with local figures attached to each. CHAI's s1-2 only has to reach a conclusion (AI is an appropriate intervention) and prescribes no workflow map, no role/decision-point granularity and no quantification of current harm; s1-3's baseline is a comparator for success measures, not an enumeration of what today's process costs.

items.text: Lay out the revised workflow as it would run once the AI system is in place.

attrs.residue: A documented to-be workflow: the exact point at which the model's result enters the care pathway, who receives it, who acts on it, which existing step it replaces or augments, and an explicit delta against the as-is map from item 1.2 - written by the adopting clinician during need specification, before any solution is chosen. CHAI's s2-1 requires only that end users participated in design (a process assurance, not a workflow document), s2-2 documents intended use, users and setting rather than the integration point and the step displaced, and s2-5 covers only the oversight and override branch of the flow.

items.text: Say what kind of result the system is expected to produce — generated prose, a probability or category derived from input data, or an estimate of how an outcome would shift under a given intervention — bearing in mind that each of these commits the project to a different analytic approach.

attrs.residue: An up-front commitment to the class of result required - generated prose, a predicted probability or class derived from inputs, or a causal estimate of how an outcome shifts under an intervention - together with an acknowledgment that the choice fixes which modeling and evaluation family applies downstream. CHAI never asks the adopter to declare an output class during need specification; s2-2 documents intended use and out-of-scope uses without naming the analytic type, and the model card's outputs and model-type fields are a developer's description of a finished product rather than a specification the adopter commits to beforehand.

items.text: Which performance measures actually matter for this use, and how good do the numbers have to be before adoption is defensible? Statistical or data-science input is worth soliciting here.

attrs.residue: A minimum acceptable numeric value attached to each named metric, chosen to suit the output class declared in 1.4, with the clinical reasoning for where each bar was placed - functioning as a pre-committed adoption go/no-go yardstick that later chapters test candidate solutions against. s1-3 requires success measures and a baseline but no acceptance floor and no justification of its level; s2-4's clinically justified thresholds are the model's operating points (where to alert or classify), which is a different quantity, set at design stage on a system already chosen.

items.text: Can the gain expected from rolling this out be expressed in numbers?

attrs.residue: An ex-ante, quantified projection of benefit - events averted, clinician or patient time saved, cost avoided, throughput gained - with the assumptions behind the figure exposed, or an explicit reasoned record that quantification is not feasible and why, produced before the decision to adopt. Every CHAI value question is backward-looking: s1-3 defines what will be measured without estimating its size, s6-6 re-evaluates realized value after go-live, and s5-3 measures real-world effect during the pilot. None asks for a prospective estimate, its assumptions, or a documented null answer.

sections.title: Exploring alternative solutions
sections.purpose: Check the proposed system against everything else that could meet the same need, so the choice rests on a documented comparison rather than on the first option that came to the organization's attention.

items.text: Survey what else already addresses this need — commercial offerings, approaches reported in the literature, and tools built in-house — and record what each one does and what it would cost. Procurement or business-development help may be useful here.

attrs.residue: A documented landscape scan drawing on all three sources - the vendor market, the published literature, and internally buildable options - listing each candidate with its key capabilities, maturity and deployment status, its acquisition cost and its ongoing cost of ownership, and recording an empty result as a deliberate finding rather than silence. s1-2 only has to show that AI is an appropriate intervention rather than merely a possible one; it requires no inventory of competing solutions, no coverage of the literature or in-house build option, and CHAI contains no cost or cost-of-ownership requirement anywhere in its 41 criteria.

items.text: Where alternatives do exist, how do they compare on performance, and does any of them clear the bar set in item 1.5?

When more than one option would be acceptable, what actually separates them? Identify what each brings that the others do not, and any distinguishing feature that tips the decision toward one of them.

sections.title: Population characterization
sections.purpose: Establish who the model was built on and whether those patients plausibly stand in for the people this organization would actually run it on.

items.text: Identify whose records went into building the model: the eligibility and disqualification rules that bounded the cohort, plus a profile of the care environment those patients were drawn from.

attrs.residue: The enrollment and exclusion rules actually applied to bound the cohort, plus a structured profile of the originating care environment (geography, inpatient versus ambulatory, specialty, number of contributing sites, calendar window). s3-1 names sources and limitations but not the eligibility logic that produced the cohort.

items.text: State how many patients the development cohort contained.

attrs.residue: An explicit patient count, with record or encounter counts and per-split and per-site breakdowns, reported so cohort scale can be weighed against the modeling approach and parameter count. CHAI carries size only as one word inside a model card field and never asks for per-partition or per-site numbers.

items.text: Summarize what that cohort looked like, reporting the spread of its principal variables the way a baseline-characteristics table would.

attrs.residue: Clinical content beyond demographics, namely comorbidity burden and the principal clinical variables, and the statistical form of the summary: counts and percentages for categorical fields, central tendency with dispersion for continuous ones. s3-2 stops at demographic and socio-demographic make-up.

items.text: Explain the partitioning scheme that separated patients into fitting, tuning, and held-out evaluation groups.

Check that each subgroup whose care could differ was represented in sufficient numbers to support a claim about it. Which subgroups matter is use-case specific, and typically includes disease severity strata, deprivation or payer status, and the usual demographic axes.

attrs.residue: An adequacy verdict: per-subgroup counts and proportions weighed against what reliable downstream performance estimates require, with an explicit naming of the strata too sparse to support them. CHAI reports composition (s3-2) and names which subgroups to evaluate (s2-3) but never asks whether the development data hold enough of each group for those evaluations to mean anything.

items.text: From a clinician's standpoint, decide whether the people and care context behind the model's training and testing resemble the patients this organization would apply it to.

attrs.residue: A named clinician's reasoned comparison of the development cohort and its care context against the local target population, itemizing concrete divergences in case mix, disease prevalence, demographic profile and level of care, and closing with an explicit tolerable-or-disqualifying verdict. s4-1 asks for local validation results, not for a documented cohort-gap appraisal, and gives no point at which a mismatch stops the project.

sections.title: Input data
sections.purpose: Pin down exactly what the model consumes, then verify the organization can supply all of it, in the right form, at the moment of execution.

items.text: Enumerate every variable the model consumes, and for the development data describe how each was captured and how its values were spread.

attrs.residue: A variable-by-variable inventory of every model input, each with how that particular value was captured (device, assay, structured form, free text) and its distribution in the development data. s3-1 and the inputSource field describe the data source as a whole and require neither a per-feature inventory nor per-feature training distributions.

items.text: Specify the shape and encoding in which the model requires its inputs to arrive.
Pin down the moment in the care process at which the model is meant to fire, which doubles as the cutoff beyond which no input may be used.

attrs.residue: A named trigger event or timestamp at which the solution fires, the lookback window for input collection, and the explicit rule that nothing recorded after that instant may feed the model. This boundary is what prevents target leakage during development and mistimed inputs in production; s2-2's intended-use documentation never requires it to be stated.

items.text: Describe the treatment of absent values when the model was fitted, and prescribe how absences should be treated once it is running live.

attrs.residue: The production rule: how missingness must be handled at inference, and the conditions under which the system should withhold a prediction rather than issue one. s3-4 documents the training-time strategy only, and the model card has no data-handling field, so the runtime suppression rule has no home in CHAI at all.

items.text: Describe the treatment of out-of-range or outlying values during fitting, and the rule to apply to them in production.

attrs.residue: Documented out-of-range handling: plausibility ranges, clipping or winsorization bounds and transformations applied during fitting, plus the defined runtime behavior when a live value falls outside the accepted range. s3-4 names checks at development time and prescribes nothing for production.

items.text: From a clinical viewpoint, judge whether the model is being fed the information a clinician would consider essential for the job it is meant to do.
Audit the organization's own data holdings for each input the model needs, confirm they can be supplied in the required encoding, and profile how those variables are distributed and captured locally.

attrs.residue: A per-input audit against the organization's own repositories: the source system serving each required variable, flagged format and terminology mismatches, and local distributions and collection practice for the inputs that do exist. s1-7 scopes what data are needed and permitted without verifying any of it against local systems, and s4-1 arrives far too late to redirect the build.

items.text: Confirm each required input will actually be on hand at the moment and in the setting where the model is supposed to run, not merely present somewhere in retrospective archives.

attrs.residue: Per-input confirmation that each required value is genuinely on hand at the moment and place of execution: delivery latency, the system serving it at the point of care, and explicit identification of any variable that exists only in retrospective archives or arrives after the trigger point. CHAI has no pre-build availability gate, so under s2-7 and s4-4 this failure surfaces only at shadow evaluation.

items.text: Weigh whether the value distributions of the developer's training inputs sit close enough to the locally observed ones for a clinician to be comfortable.

attrs.residue: A side-by-side comparison of the developer's training distributions against locally observed ones for each key input, performed before deployment and closed by a named clinician's verdict that the shifts are acceptable or disqualifying. s4-1 measures performance and s6-1 watches drift after go-live; no criterion requires the input-distribution gap analysis itself or a clinical sign-off on it.

items.text: Weigh whether the way the training inputs were generated and recorded matches how this organization generates and records them.

attrs.residue: An adopter-side clinical comparison of how the data are generated and recorded on each side (instruments, assay platforms, imaging protocols, coding habits, and who records what and when), ending in a verdict on whether the two processes are comparable enough. s3-1 documents the developer's provenance and stops there; the comparison itself is unassigned in CHAI.

sections.title: Output data
sections.purpose: Characterize what the model emits and the target it was trained against, then check that same target exists locally and behaves similarly.

items.text: State what the model emits, in two parts: the substance of the result (for example a written summary, a continuous risk estimate, or a category assigned to a clinical finding) and its data type (free text, numeric, or categorical).

attrs.residue: A full output specification: the semantic meaning of the result, its variable type, value range or scale or label set, units, and how many outputs are produced per invocation. s2-4 fixes an operating point on an output it never requires to be specified, and the outputs card field is free text with no required content.

items.text: Explain how the target the model learns to produce was operationalized, and give its key descriptive properties, for example how frequently the labeled event occurred.

attrs.residue: The operational definition of the target: code sets and phenotyping logic, the annotation or adjudication procedure with inter-rater agreement where humans labeled, plus the base rate or value distribution of that target in the development data. CHAI has no label-definition criterion and no model-card field for ground truth, so how the outcome was constructed and how reliably it was captured stay invisible.

items.text: Where the model forecasts something, state the window over which the forecast event was ascertained.
Judge clinically whether the target the model was taught to produce, as characterized in the three preceding items, is both pertinent to the stated need and dependable as a label.

attrs.residue: A clinician's appraisal of the developer's training target as characterized in 5.1 to 5.3: whether that operational definition genuinely stands in for what clinicians care about rather than a convenient proxy, and whether it was captured accurately enough to be trusted as ground truth. s1-1 settles an outcome at the problem-definition stage and is never revisited against the developer's actual label.

items.text: Determine whether the organization's own data carry the model's target variable too, and if so profile it against the properties the developer reported.

attrs.residue: A statement of local target availability and how it is ascertained, with its descriptive properties, above all the local event rate, expressed so they can be set directly against the developer's reported figures. s4-1 presumes local outcome data rather than requiring them to be found and profiled, and s1-3's baseline concerns the process being improved, not the model's label.

items.text: Weigh whether the target's distribution locally sits close enough to the developer's reported distribution for a clinician to accept.

attrs.residue: A direct comparison of the local outcome distribution, chiefly event rate, against the developer's reported distribution, plus a documented clinical verdict on whether the gap would undermine calibration, the chosen operating threshold, or clinical usefulness. s4-3 is an after-the-fact measurement on an already-assembled system, not a pre-adoption judgment on prevalence shift.

sections.title: Development process
sections.purpose: Open up how the model was actually built so that a reviewer can judge whether the training methodology was sound and free of the classic traps that inflate apparent quality.

items.text: Describe the modeling approach behind the solution and how it was fitted — which family of algorithm it belongs to and what the training procedure looked like.
Confirm that the algorithm class chosen is a sensible match for the kind of output the solution emits.
Where the solution forecasts a future event, explain how subjects whose observation ended early were treated during training, and confirm that this was handled deliberately rather than by default.

attrs.residue: How subjects whose observation window ended early were treated when the training labels were formed - exclusion, censoring-aware loss, competing-risk modeling or imputation - together with the argument that the chosen treatment does not systematically distort the outcome definition.

items.text: Explain the safeguards that kept information about the outcome from contaminating the predictor variables, and confirm this risk was actively tested for rather than assumed away.
Describe what was done to detect and reduce inequitable or skewed behavior across groups, and confirm the issue received deliberate attention during development.

attrs.residue: The developer's development-time fairness assessment in full: which groups were examined, which disparity measures were computed, and which performance gaps remained unresolved after mitigation was applied.

items.text: State whether practicing clinicians and other subject-matter specialists took part in building the solution, and in what capacity.

attrs.residue: Named clinical and domain contributors to the model's construction and the specific build activities they shaped - outcome and label definition, feature selection, error case review.

sections.title: Performance
sections.purpose: Establish what the solution's accuracy actually is — as reported, as benchmarked against alternatives, as re-tested on local data, and as observed in a pilot — and whether it clears the bar the clinical lead set at the outset.

items.text: Report how well the solution scored on historical data, using measures appropriate to the kind of model it is.

attrs.residue: The developer's own retrospective performance figures on its evaluation data, with metrics matched to the output type and reported with uncertainty intervals.

items.text: Break those measured results down across the patient subgroups that matter clinically.

attrs.residue: Stratified metric tables from the developer's own evaluation cohort, covering strata CHAI does not name - comorbidity burden and care site - alongside the demographic ones.

items.text: Characterize the dataset on which these results were measured.

attrs.residue: A characterization of the held-out evaluation cohort as such - size, time span, source sites, inclusion and exclusion rules, outcome prevalence, and the mechanism that kept it separate from the data used to fit the model.

items.text: State whether the evaluation sample preserves the real-world balance of outcomes or was deliberately resampled, since rebalancing distorts any metric that depends on how common the outcome is.
Report any evaluation carried out in settings beyond the one that supplied the training data, and what the results were there.

attrs.residue: The supplier's disclosure of whether validation outside the training setting has ever been performed, naming the host setting and data source and giving the results - or an explicit statement that no such validation exists.

items.text: Share any evidence of how the solution has behaved in live clinical use elsewhere, including where that experience comes from.
Judge whether the reported results clear the metric thresholds the clinical lead specified when the need was first defined.

attrs.residue: A recorded pass or fail verdict by the clinical lead setting the supplier's reported metrics side by side with the acceptance thresholds fixed when the clinical need was first defined, with the reasoning behind the call.

items.text: Assess whether these results look credible and competitive when set beside the alternative solutions surveyed earlier.
Determine whether the organization's own historical records could support an in-house evaluation of the solution, and estimate what mounting one would cost in effort.

attrs.residue: A feasibility determination that the inputs and outcome data a local evaluation would need actually exist in the organization's historical records, plus a concrete estimate of the data-engineering work, elapsed time and staff it would consume.

items.text: If an in-house retrospective test goes ahead, confirm whether the data it would consume match exactly what the live system would actually receive at runtime.

attrs.residue: A field-by-field confirmation that retrospectively extracted inputs match what the live system would receive at run time, naming any divergence in timing, completeness, source system or coding that would make the retrospective result optimistic.

items.text: Where a local retrospective test was actually carried out, give the clinical verdict on whether its results were good enough.

attrs.residue: The clinical expert's explicit sufficiency verdict on the local retrospective results, measured against the thresholds set at the outset - or, where no local evaluation was mounted, a recorded reason why it was not.

items.text: Where a limited trial run was judged worthwhile before full rollout, summarize what it revealed about accuracy, day-to-day workability and how users received it.

attrs.residue: A single consolidated pilot report that also carries the solution's measured predictive accuracy during the live run and ends in an explicit recommendation on whether to proceed to wider deployment.

sections.title: Explainability
sections.purpose: Determine whether the solution can account for its outputs both model-wide and case by case, and whether those accounts stand up to clinical scrutiny.

items.text: Identify which variables drive the model's behavior overall, or account for why such a ranking cannot be produced.

attrs.residue: A model-wide ranking of the variables driving behavior with the attribution method named - coefficients, SHAP, permutation importance, attention summaries - or a technical justification for why global attribution cannot be produced for this model class.

items.text: State whether the solution can justify the result it produces for one specific case, and illustrate with worked examples spanning different kinds of patients.

attrs.residue: Demonstrated per-case explanation output, accompanied by worked sample explanations across a deliberately varied case mix - typical, borderline, atypical, and cases the model got wrong.

items.text: Give a clinician's verdict on whether the model-wide and per-case explanations hold up medically.

attrs.residue: A clinical critique of the substance of the explanations: whether the identified drivers are physiologically plausible, whether any look like artifacts or proxies for something else, and whether a clinician could reasonably act on them.

sections.title: Regulations, data security & privacy
sections.purpose: Confirm the solution can be fielded lawfully and safely — regulatory conformity, honesty with patients, protection of data against attack, and respect for privacy rules.

items.text: Establish whether the solution satisfies the regulatory rules that apply in this jurisdiction and this institution, drawing on legal counsel and the information security lead.

attrs.residue: A compliance determination made at the assessment point: the clearances or approvals actually held, the device classification and declared intended use mapped against applicable institutional, local and national requirements, with legal counsel's and the information-security lead's sign-off recorded.

items.text: Decide whether patients are told clearly enough that an algorithm plays a part in their care, with legal input on what disclosure is actually owed.

attrs.residue: The disclosure itself and a test of its legal sufficiency: the notice wording, where and when patients encounter it, any consent or opt-out arrangement, and counsel's opinion that what patients are told is in fact enough.

items.text: Verify that the solution meets the institution's requirements for safeguarding data and withstanding attack, with the information security lead involved.
Confirm that the solution's handling of identifiable information satisfies the privacy rules that apply locally, again with the information security lead involved.

attrs.residue: A formal privacy-conformity determination against local privacy rules - lawful basis for processing, data minimization, retention and deletion schedules, any cross-border transfer, and any secondary or vendor reuse of patient data - with documented sign-off.

sections.title: Deployment plan
sections.purpose: Pins down how the solution will actually be wired into clinical work and into the organization's technical stack - where it surfaces, who acts on it, and what has to be built to serve it.

items.text: Pinpoint where along the care pathway the tool fires - which encounter, decision point, or step of the existing process it attaches to.

attrs.residue: The exact trigger moment within the adopting site's existing care process - which encounter, decision point or process step the output attaches to - stated as a local integration commitment consistent with the redesigned workflow, rather than as a generic statement of intended care setting.

items.text: Name the host application or screen where clinicians will actually see the result, and describe how using it is meant to feel day to day - how discoverable it is, how many clicks it costs, how reliably it is on hand.

attrs.residue: Naming the receiving information system and the specific screen or display surface, plus a stated target user experience - placement, discoverability, interaction cost, availability and how intrusive the presentation is - fixed in advance as a design target rather than assessed after the fact in a pilot.

items.text: State whether a named human clinician stands between the model and the patient, owning the choice to act on a result or set it aside.

attrs.residue: An explicit statement of whether a named clinical role receives each result and owns the accountable decision to act on it or set it aside, where accountability for the resulting care decision sits, and - where no human is in the loop - a reasoned justification for operating autonomously. CHAI's s2-5 presumes an oversight path exists and never entertains or requires the case for running without one.

items.text: If each result has to arrive with its rationale attached, work out how that supporting explanation gets rendered inside the host system next to the result itself.

attrs.residue: A decision on whether an explanation must accompany every output and, where it must, a concrete rendering design: where in the host information system the supporting rationale appears relative to the result, in what format, and how it is technically carried there. CHAI never addresses how explanations reach the screen.

items.text: Determine whether fresh interfaces or middleware must be built to carry results from whatever serves the model over to the system that will display them.

attrs.residue: A build-versus-exists gap analysis across the link from the service producing outputs to the system displaying them - which interfaces, message formats and pipeline components are already available and which must be newly developed - produced before the organization commits.

items.text: Identify the host hardware the model will execute on and confirm its compute and memory headroom are adequate for the expected load.

attrs.residue: Naming the execution host and sizing it - a capacity assessment of memory, CPU/GPU and throughput headroom weighed against projected inference volume. CHAI never asks whether the infrastructure can carry the expected load.

items.text: Confirm that every input feed reaches that execution environment promptly enough to be useful, and flag which feeds must arrive live rather than on a batch schedule.

attrs.residue: A per-input timeliness analysis showing each feed reaches the execution environment early enough for the designated inference moment, with refresh rates stated and feeds that must arrive live explicitly separated from scheduled or batched ones.

sections.title: Monitoring plan
sections.purpose: Establishes how the system will be watched once live, so that drift in its inputs, its outputs, its accuracy, or the underlying medical knowledge is caught rather than discovered late.

items.text: From the builder's standpoint, state the cadence at which the model has to be refreshed or refit.

attrs.residue: A developer-declared retraining or refit interval stated up front, together with the technical reasoning behind it - expected data drift, or decay observed in earlier deployments.

items.text: Say whether the system refits itself automatically in the field, and if it does, describe how each refreshed version's quality gets verified before it influences care.

attrs.residue: A yes/no on self-updating or online learning in production and, where it applies, the governance gate and performance-verification procedure applied to every automatically regenerated model version before it is allowed to influence care.

items.text: Lay out how incoming feature values will be watched for drift or outright breakage once the system is running.

attrs.residue: A field-level input-monitoring design committed before launch: which specific feature values and distributions are tracked, at what sampling frequency, and what distinguishes drift from outright breakage of a feed. CHAI names neither the monitored fields nor the frequency.

items.text: Lay out the equivalent watch on what the model emits, so that shifts in the distribution of its results surface early.

attrs.residue: An output-monitoring design naming the statistics tracked on what the model emits - score distribution, positive or alert rate - the cadence at which they are reviewed, and the specific triggers that escalate a distribution shift, all specified before go-live.

items.text: From the clinical side, state how often the medical content baked into the solution - guidelines, thresholds, standards of care - needs refreshing.

attrs.residue: A clinically driven refresh interval for the medical knowledge the solution encodes - guidelines, decision thresholds, standards of care - justified by how fast that knowledge is moving, and stated separately from the developer's retraining interval so the two can diverge.

items.text: Set out how the solution's accuracy will keep being measured after go-live, not only before it.

attrs.residue: Naming the source of post-deployment ground truth or outcome labels against which accuracy will keep being computed, together with the measurement intervals and the named people who review the results. CHAI assumes performance can be measured after go-live without asking how truth is obtained.

sections.title: Evaluation plan
sections.purpose: Settles in advance how the deployment's real-world benefit and harm will be measured, fed back and reported.

items.text: Define what counts as success for this rollout - the outcome measures the deployment itself will be judged on.
Describe the study design that will test whether the rollout genuinely helped - and whether it harmed anyone along the way.

attrs.residue: A pre-specified evaluation methodology that treats benefit and unintended harm as one design question: comparator, measures and analysis approach, at the level of rigor that lets the result be believed rather than merely recorded.

items.text: Check whether the rollout itself can be structured up front - staggered, randomized, phased by site - so that its effect can later be measured credibly.

attrs.residue: An explicit decision on structuring the rollout so its effect can later be attributed - randomization, stepped-wedge, or deliberate site-by-site phasing - or a documented reason why no such design is feasible here. CHAI never asks that the rollout sequence itself be arranged to make the effect measurable.

items.text: Decide how you will capture what users actually think of it - perceived usefulness, friction, trust.

attrs.residue: A named mechanism for collecting subjective user input - survey instrument, structured interview, or in-application feedback - with stated timing and sampling, designed before go-live and running continuously rather than as a one-off pilot assessment.

items.text: Decide who writes up the evaluation findings, how often, and to whom they go.

attrs.residue: A reporting plan for the ongoing evaluation itself - who writes it up, in what format, at what cadence, and which governance body or audience receives it - covering routine effectiveness and benefit findings, not only safety events and scheduled audits.

sections.title: Organizational AI strategy fit
sections.purpose: Gives the organization's AI leadership the final word on the quality of the answers, the merit of the solution, and its fit with the wider AI strategy.

items.text: Step back and judge how well the rest of the checklist was actually answered - depth, candor, and what was left open.
Give an overall opinion on the proposed system itself, and on whether it genuinely answers the need stated at the very outset.

attrs.residue: A recorded holistic opinion from a leader with organization-wide AI visibility on the finished proposed solution, delivered at the close of the appraisal and judged explicitly against the clinical need and performance requirements set at the very start - an appraisal of the proposal, not the up-front analysis that produced it.

items.text: Judge the fit with where the organization is heading on AI overall, including knock-on effects that reach beyond this one deployment.
